newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. fails to persuade Japan on food to N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: U.S. fails to persuade Japan on food to N.Korea.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeline Albright failed on Sunday to persuade Japan to join it in giving food aid to the tottering regime in famine-hit North Korea, Japanese officials said.

In a rare foreign policy difference between the two close allies, Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told Albright reports of North Korean abduction of Japanese citizens stood in the way of giving food aid to North Korea at present.

Earlier this month the Japanese government said nine Japanese citizens may have been abducted by North Korean agents and taken to the communist country in the past while two others barely escaped kidnap attempts.
The World Food Programme has estimated North Korea needs 2.3 million tonnes of grain this year to compensate for poor harvests as a result of devastating 1995 and 1996 floods.
But it appealed recently only for $41.5 million -- equal to 100,000 tonnes -- because that was all the U.N. agency felt it could raise from South Korea and other key states at this time.
Washington has pledged $10 million and Seoul $6 million.
Japan has held back so far from committing itself to new aid because of the controversy over reports that agents from the communist nation have kidnapped Japanese citizens.

The reports, which have been denied by Pyongyang, said those kidnapped were put to work giving Japanese-language training to North Korean agents so that they could travel to carry out sabotage attacks.
The most high-profile case involves a 13-year-old girl who Japanese media say was abducted 20 years ago and taken to North Korea to help teach North Korean spies how to speak Japanese.
Megumi Yokota went missing in 1977 on her way back from school in a coastal village in Niigata Prefecture, central Japan, the reports said.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has promised parliament the government will investigate the incident.
Urged by Albright to join Washington and Seoul in giving food aid. Ikeda said Japan preferred at this stage to watch how the WFP appeal worked out.

"There is the issue of the alleged kidnapped junior high school girl (Megumi Yokota) and Japan has not yet been able to find an opportunity to start normalisation talks with North Korea," Ikeda explained.
Japanese officials said that in response Albright again urged Tokyo to consider giving food aid, maybe not immediately, but at least in the future.
North Korea's reported abductions of Japanese citizens have clouded efforts to establish diplomatic relations between the two countries. Tokyo and Seoul established diplomatic ties in 1965.
In 1992, Tokyo and Pyongyang broke off normalisation talks when North Korea rejected Tokyo's demand for information about a Japanese woman it alleged was abducted by North Korean agents.

Kim Hyong-hui, a self-confessed North Korean spy who blew up a South Korean airliner in 1987, said the instructor who taught her Japanese language and customs was a Japanese woman called Yaeko Taguchi, who went missing in 1978, working under the pseudonym Lee Un-hye.
